name: Transportation
blurb: Autonomous driving is the visible front; AI also runs freight matching, maritime navigation, transit, and aviation, from IMO and EASA to the trucking, shipping, and aviation majors.

points.name: Waymo publishes its safety record

points.desc: The International Maritime Organization's MASS work - Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships - is where international rules for AI navigation, collision avoidance, and crewless vessels are being written.
points.name: The IMO governs autonomous shipping

points.desc: The FAA's innovation work and EASA's AI roadmap are the regulatory record for AI flight systems, automated risk management, and eVTOL certification - nothing flies commercially without them.
points.name: FAA and EASA gate aviation AI

points.desc: The American Trucking Associations is the industry body tracking policy and adoption for autonomous freight and AI logistics.
points.name: ATA tracks autonomous trucking policy

points.desc: The pure-play autonomous trucking platforms operating Level 4 freight on commercial highway corridors - their own operations pages are the deployment record.
points.name: Aurora and Kodiak run the driverless corridors

points.desc: C.H. Robinson applies AI to load matching, dynamic pricing, and multi-modal route optimization at one of the largest freight networks.
points.name: Freight brokerage runs on prediction

points.desc: Wärtsilä's vessel-optimization and autonomous-navigation technology is the commercial maritime AI record; Maersk applies AI across global route and port-congestion prediction.
points.name: Maritime AI ships from the equipment makers

points.desc: Airbus's innovation programs and Boeing's autonomy work cover AI flight management and predictive maintenance for commercial aircraft.
points.name: Aviation incumbents test AI in the cockpit and the hangar

points.name: Palantir is tracked on this site

summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau, AI adoption in Transportation and Warehousing stood at 10.2% as of the latest survey period, down from 11.2% in the prior period. This figure represents firms answering yes to having used AI in the preceding two weeks, capturing a snapshot of active deployment rather than strategic investment alone.

Autonomous vehicle technology dominates the visible frontier. Aurora operates the Aurora Driver, a Level 4 autonomous freight system integrated into the Volvo VNL Autonomous, running pilot corridors between Fort Worth and El Paso with professional driver partners. The company frames autonomous trucks as addressing a structural need: freight volumes are projected to grow five fold between 2010 and 2050, making autonomous transport framed as a necessity rather than optional. Waymo, originating from the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009, has served fully autonomous rides since 2015 and frames autonomous driving technology as a solution to road safety, supporting the U.S. Department of Transportation's National Roadway Safety Strategy and the Vision Zero Network's goal of eliminating traffic fatalities. However, no commercially operating, internationally trading cargo ships currently operate autonomously or remotely controlled, though successful trials have demonstrated feasibility.

Regulatory infrastructure is crystallizing across modes. The International Maritime Organization adopted the Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships Code in May 2026, effective July 1, 2026, establishing a goal-based, technology-neutral framework for design, operation, and certification. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency published its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0, outlining vision and a comprehensive action plan for safety and ethical considerations of AI in aviation, framed as a living document to be amended annually. These regulatory bodies are setting the pace for how autonomous and AI-assisted systems integrate into existing safety regimes.

Fleet telematics represents deployed AI at operational scale. Samsara's connected operations platform serves 20,000+ operations with AI-driven alerts, predictive analytics, and cameras that have prevented 380,000+ accidents through real-time in-cab alerts, automated coaching, and drowsiness detection. C.H. Robinson, a major freight broker, applies AI to load matching, dynamic pricing, and multi-modal route optimization, describing the result as autonomous logistics orchestration where supply chains analyze, decide, execute, and improve continuously across each shipment. Wärtsilä, a marine equipment maker, markets AI-driven predictive analytics for decarbonization alongside vessel-optimization technology.

The regulatory posture across transportation modes reflects cautious advancement: maritime rules are voluntary guidance designed to facilitate future mandatory instruments, aviation agencies are building frameworks in real time, and trucking operates under existing commercial motor vehicle law with industry bodies like the American Trucking Associations tracking policy. Organizations deploying AI in transportation should expect safety methodology and transparency to be competitive requirements, regulatory engagement to precede or accompany deployment at scale, and that adoption remains concentrated in freight logistics, fleet monitoring, and route optimization rather than end-to-end autonomous passenger or cargo movement outside controlled corridors.
